en.title: Informal greetings and farewells
en.summary: How to greet and say goodbye to friends, family and people of your own age.

paragraphs: With friends and family, English greetings are short and relaxed. Sam meets his friend Kate on the street.

lines.speaker: Kate
lines.text: Not bad, thanks. How about you?

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Pretty good. What are you up to this weekend?

lines.speaker: Kate
lines.text: Not much. I'm meeting my sister on Saturday.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Nice. Well, I have to go. See you later!

paragraphs: **1. Informal speech uses short forms.** The verb be and the verb have lose a letter and attach to the word before it with an apostrophe: How is it going? becomes How's it going? In writing, use short forms in friendly messages, but not in formal letters. See Introduction to Grammar: Present tense, being and having.

blocks.html:
Full formShort form
How is it going?How's it going?
I am meeting my sister.I'm meeting my sister.
What is up?What's up?

paragraphs: **2. A name after a greeting is separated by a comma.** Hi, Kate! and Bye, Sam. are written with a comma before the name. See Introduction to Grammar: Propositions and phrases.

items: **Hi** and **hey** are common. **Hello** is a little more careful.
**How's it going?** and **What's up?** are greetings. People usually answer **Fine, thanks** or **Not bad**.
Informal goodbyes include **See you later**, **Take care** and **Cheers**.

paragraphs: English speakers often say **How are you?** as a greeting and do not expect a long answer. It is polite to ask the same question back.
